stimulus.attribution: Paraphrased from Stephen G. Kurtz, The Presidency of John Adams: The Collapse of Federalism, 1795-1800 (1957).
stimulus.text: In Virginia, the Federalists campaigned for the administration with great energy after the Republicans attacked the Jay Treaty. According to an eyewitness, John Marshall led the effort, constantly warning of the horrors of war, and weeks of petitioning and public meetings culminated in resolutions demanding the treaty's execution. Although many New Yorkers backed the Republican demand for the treaty's negotiation papers, Republican agitation had not roused public opinion enough to drive the Federalists from power. The great groundswell came only after Washington entered the fray: the Republicans made a tragic blunder in letting the sanctity of Washington's name become a political football, which the Federalists were quick to exploit.

parts: A. Briefly explain one claim the author makes about the Federalists' defense of the Jay Treaty.
B. Briefly explain one reason for the rise of political parties between 1789 and 1800 that is not discussed in the excerpt.
C. Briefly explain one outcome for the Federalist Party after 1800.
exemplar: Kurtz claims the Federalists won the battle over the Jay Treaty by rallying behind Washington's prestige; the Republicans blundered by attacking Washington's name, letting Federalists pose as defenders of national honor.

Disagreement over Hamilton's financial program - the Bank, assumption of state debts, and tariffs - drove party formation, as Jefferson and Madison organized opposition to policies they saw as favoring elites.
After losing the election of 1800, the Federalists declined into a sectional New England party and effectively died after the Hartford Convention of 1814-1815 discredited them as disloyal.

stimulus.attribution: Paraphrased from William R. Castle, Under Secretary of State, address to the Women's National Republican Club, 1932.
stimulus.text: Germany could not make the payments due on July 1, and without those payments America's own debtors, strained by the Depression, could hardly pay the United States. Financial collapse at this vulnerable point could drag down neighboring countries. Germany was not permanently ruined - Germans do not give up - so the nation had to be saved to take its place again as a safeguard against disorder. If Germany could not buy, prices of foodstuffs, cotton, and minerals would fall further; if revolution came, holders of German securities worldwide would suffer. Germany was the key spot: with her rescue, the tide might turn for everyone.

parts: A. Briefly describe one policy response of the American government to the European financial crisis described in the passage.
B. Briefly describe one effect of the Great Depression on American foreign policy from 1929 to 1945 that is not mentioned in the passage.
C. Briefly explain one change in American foreign policy after 1945.
exemplar: President Hoover proposed the 1931 Hoover Moratorium, suspending war-debt and reparations payments for a year to stabilize European finances.
The Depression deepened American isolationism, leading Congress to pass the Neutrality Acts of the 1930s banning arms sales and loans to belligerents.
After 1945 the United States abandoned isolationism for sustained global engagement, building Cold War alliances such as NATO (1949) and funding European recovery through the Marshall Plan.

stimulus.attribution: Described from 'Map of the United States in 1803,' U.S. National Archives and Records Administration.
stimulus.text: The map shows the Louisiana Purchase territory (shaded) ceded by France to the United States by the treaty of April 30, 1803, stretching from the Mississippi River west to the Rocky Mountains and from the Gulf of Mexico north to British Canada. The existing United States lies east of the Mississippi, with Spanish territory to the west and southwest.

parts: A. Briefly explain what the map shows about the territorial growth of the United States by 1803.
B. Briefly explain how the map illustrates the significance of the Louisiana Purchase.
C. Briefly explain one political controversy caused by the territorial acquisition shown on the map.
exemplar: The map shows the Purchase roughly doubling the nation's area, adding a vast territory west of the Mississippi between the existing states and Spanish lands.
The shaded Purchase dwarfs the original states, showing how one treaty instantly made the United States a continental-scale power controlling the Mississippi River's western bank.
The acquisition revived the debate over whether slavery would expand into the new territory, a controversy that produced the Missouri Compromise of 1820.
